text: Today's paper, Rethinking Circuit Evaluation, asks whether circuits explain a model's mistakes. This video asks whether the answer can be explained away.
say: Today's paper, Rethinking Circuit Evaluation, asks whether circuits explain a model's mistakes. This video asks whether the answer can be explained away.
heard: Today's paper, Rethinking Circuit Evaluation, asks whether circuits explain a model's mistakes. This video asks whether the answer can be explained away.

text: A circuit is a small part of a network that is supposed to explain how the whole network does a task. The paper scores it against the model, not against the right answer.
say: A circuit is a small part of a network that is supposed to explain how the whole network does a task. The paper scores it against the model, not against the right answer.
heard: A circuit is a small part of a network that is supposed to explain how the whole network does a task. The paper scores it against the model, not against the right answer.

text: Take a thousand test sentences. The model gets fewer than one percent of them wrong.
say: Take a thousand test sentences. The model gets fewer than one percent of them wrong.
heard: Take a thousand test sentences. The model gets fewer than 1% of them wrong.

text: Split them into two piles: the sentences the model gets right, and the ones it gets wrong.
say: Split them into two piles: the sentences the model gets right, and the ones it gets wrong.
heard: Split them into two piles, the sentences the model gets right and the ones it gets wrong.

text: On the first pile, agreement means the circuit is right too. That's correct agreement.
say: On the first pile, agreement means the circuit is right too. That's correct agreement.
heard: On the first pile, agreement means the circuit is right, too. That's correct agreement.

text: On the second, it means the circuit makes the exact same mistake. That's error agreement.
say: On the second, it means the circuit makes the exact same mistake. That's error agreement.
heard: On the second, it means the circuit makes the exact same mistake. That's error agreement.

text: Take a famous circuit in GPT-2 small, for what I'll call the name task: picking who receives something in a sentence.
say: Take a famous circuit in G P T two small, for what I'll call the name task: picking who receives something in a sentence.
heard: Take a famous circuit in GPT too small for what I'll call the name task, picking who receives something in a sentence.

text: On the first pile, it agrees with the model ninety-nine point five percent of the time.
say: On the first pile, it agrees with the model ninety-nine point five percent of the time.
heard: On the first pile, it agrees with the model 99.5% of the time.

text: On the second pile, only fifteen percent. Whenever you see a gap like that, look for a boring explanation. The paper tests three.
say: On the second pile, only fifteen percent. Whenever you see a gap like that, look for a boring explanation. The paper tests three.
heard: On the second pile, only 15%. Whenever you see a gap like that, look for a boring explanation. The paper tests three.

text: Boring explanation one: errors are rare. If a method almost never sees a mistake, it never learns to make one.
say: Boring explanation one: errors are rare. If a method almost never sees a mistake, it never learns to make one.
heard: Boring explanation one, errors are rare. If a method almost never sees a mistake, it never learns to make one.

text: So the authors test bigger models, on science questions and subtraction, where mistakes are common.
say: So the authors test bigger models, on science questions and subtraction, where mistakes are common.
heard: So the authors test bigger models on science questions and subtraction where mistakes are common.

text: Each panel goes from a tiny circuit to half the network. The solid line is agreement where the model is right. The dashed line is agreement where it's wrong.
say: Each panel goes from a tiny circuit to half the network. The solid line is agreement where the model is right. The dashed line is agreement where it's wrong.
heard: Each panel goes from a tiny circuit to half the network. The solid line is agreement where the model is right. The dashed line is agreement where it's wrong.

text: Take Gemma on the hard science questions. Thirty-eight percent of the examples used to find its circuit are its own mistakes.

text: Yet at every size shown, the dashed line stays below the solid one.

text: What if you weight the mistakes more heavily during the search?
say: What if you weight the mistakes more heavily during the search?
heard: What if you weight the mistakes more heavily during the search?

text: On the name task, giving errors half the weight raises error agreement from about nine percent to thirty-seven.
say: On the name task, giving errors half the weight raises error agreement from about nine percent to thirty-seven.

text: But agreement on the right pile falls, from about ninety-nine to ninety-one.

text: Searching on equal numbers of errors and successes makes a similar trade. So rarity is part of the story, but not all of it.

text: The second boring explanation: mistakes are close calls.
say: The second boring explanation: mistakes are close calls.
heard: The second boring explanation, mistakes are close calls.

text: When the model is wrong, the two answers often score almost the same. A near tie is easy to tip, so small differences between circuit and model flip the answer.

text: So the authors pair each mistake with a correct answer where the model was just as unsure.

text: For Llama on the hard science questions, agreement on the right pile falls from eighty percent to about forty-seven among these close calls. Error agreement stays near fifty-five.

text: Boring explanation three: the circuit is just a bit too sure of the right answer. So nudge it toward the wrong name.

text: That works, in one sense. Shift the circuit's output toward the repeated name, and it reproduces at least as many errors as more elaborate fixes.

text: You can even match how often the model is wrong.
